Question:
Positive integers \(a,\) \(b,\) and \(c\) are randomly and independently selected with replacement from the set \(\{1, 2, 3,\dots, 2010\}.\)

What is the probability that \(abc + ab + a\) is divisible by \(3?\)
Solution:
Only the remainders upon division by \(3\) matter. Since \(2010=3\cdot670\), exactly \(670\) available integers have each remainder \(0,1,2\). Independence therefore makes the \(3^3=27\) ordered remainder triples equally likely.

Factor the expression to separate the role of \(a\):
\[
abc+ab+a=a\bigl(b(c+1)+1\bigr).
\]
If \(a\) has remainder \(0\), the expression is divisible by \(3\) for every choice of the other two remainders. This gives \(3\cdot3=9\) favorable triples.

If \(a\) has remainder \(1\) or \(2\), the bracket must itself be divisible by \(3\), because a product of two nonzero remainders modulo \(3\) cannot have remainder \(0\). Examine all three possible remainders of \(c\):

If \(c\) has remainder \(0\), the bracket behaves like \(b+1\), so \(b\) must have remainder \(2\).

If \(c\) has remainder \(1\), the bracket behaves like \(2b+1\), so \(b\) must have remainder \(1\).

If \(c\) has remainder \(2\), then \(c+1\) is divisible by \(3\), leaving the bracket with remainder \(1\). This case never works.

Thus there are exactly two allowed ordered remainder pairs \((b,c)\), namely \((2,0)\) and \((1,1)\). Each works with either nonzero remainder of \(a\), giving \(2\cdot2=4\) additional triples. The cases are disjoint and cover every remainder of \(a\) and \(c\), so the probability is
\[
\frac{9+4}{27}=\boxed{\frac{13}{27}},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
